content.promptText: Some people believe household responsibilities should be shared equally among everyone living in a home, while others think they should depend on each person's schedule and abilities. Which view do you agree with, and why?

speaking.answer: I agree more with the second view, that it should depend on each person's schedule and abilities. Splitting everything equally sounds fair on paper, but real life isn't always equal. For example, if my roommate works late three nights a week, it wouldn't be reasonable to ask her to cook on those nights. Um, I'd happily take that job and then she could wash dishes on her free days. Also, people are naturally good at different things. Some enjoy cooking while others don't mind cleaning the bathroom. Honestly, what matters most is that everyone contributes something and communicates openly with each other. When people feel the arrangement is fair, there are fewer arguments, and the home feels more comfortable for everyone.

Fast fashion refers to the rapid production of inexpensive clothing for mass-market sales. Fast fashion allows consumers to buy trendy items at low prices and provides job opportunities in manufacturing countries. But critics argue that fast fashion leads to vast amounts of pollution in the form of discarded clothing, which harms the environment, and that workers experience poor working conditions. In your view, what would be the most effective solution to the problems associated with fast fashion?
content.post: Kelly: Based on my experience, today’s consumers demand products that are made in environmentally and socially responsible ways. As a result, market forces are effective at getting companies to adopt better practices voluntarily. Consumer demand can encourage positive change without the need for strict accountability being imposed on clothing makers.

writing.answer:
The most effective response to fast fashion is enforceable producer responsibility, supported by informed consumer demand. Andrew is right that brands should bear the cost of pollution and unsafe labor conditions created throughout their supply chains. Without rules, a company that ignores worker safety or dumps textile waste can sell more cheaply than a responsible competitor.

Kelly correctly notes that consumers can reward better practices. Buying durable clothing, repairing items, and checking where products were made sends a useful market signal. However, shoppers cannot investigate every subcontractor, and low-income consumers may have few affordable alternatives. Voluntary demand therefore cannot protect all workers or communities.

Governments should require supply-chain disclosure, factory inspections, minimum durability standards, and collection programs funded by clothing brands. Fees on excessive textile waste could finance recycling while making disposable production less profitable. Consumer choices would then reward companies that exceed the legal minimum, but environmental and labor protection would no longer depend on shoppers having perfect information.

content.promptText: Thanks for participating. I'd like to ask you about your musical experiences. Do you play a musical instrument or sing? If not, what would you choose to learn how to do? Piano or guitar?

speaking.answer: Actually, I don't play any instrument, but I sing a little, mostly in the shower or when I'm walking home. I took choir lessons in elementary school, and, uh, I still remember some of the songs. If I had to choose an instrument to learn, I'd pick the piano. I think it's easier to start with because you can see the notes laid out in front of you, and you can play melodies and chords at the same time. The guitar is more popular with my friends, and it's easier to carry around, but my fingers are not very strong, and I'd probably quit. Plus, a piano has such a beautiful sound. I could practice at my school's music room during lunch. I mean, one day I hope to play a favorite song for my family.

content.promptText: Thank you. Please describe one memorable experience you have had with music. What made it special?

speaking.answer: One experience I'll never forget was my first live concert. I was sixteen, and my older sister took me to see a band I'd loved for years. Um, we stood in a huge crowd, and when the first song started, everyone began singing together. I got goosebumps. Hearing the music live was so different from listening on my headphones. I could feel the bass in my chest, and the lights moved along with the songs. What made it special was being surrounded by thousands of people who all loved the same music, and I felt connected to strangers. Afterward my sister and I sang all the way home, honestly pretty badly. I still have the ticket in my drawer, and it reminds me of that night.

content.promptText: I see. When you listen to music, do you prefer to listen by yourself or with others? Why?

speaking.answer: It depends on my mood, but I think I prefer listening alone. When I'm by myself, I can choose exactly what I want, turn it up loud, and really focus on the lyrics. Um, it's also my way of relaxing after a long day, and I don't have to talk to anyone. But listening with others has its charm too. At a party or on a road trip, music brings everyone together, and you discover new songs from your friends that you'd never find yourself. I mean, I've found some of my favorite artists that way. So both are great, but if I had to choose, I'd say alone, because music feels more personal that way, like a private conversation between me and the song.

content.promptText: Some people believe that music education should be a compulsory part of school curriculum. Do you agree or disagree with this view? Please explain your reasons.

speaking.answer: I agree, and, honestly, I wish I'd had more of it in school. Music helps children in many ways. It teaches them to listen carefully, to be patient, and to work with others, especially in a choir or band. It also helps with memory, because learning a piece means remembering notes, rhythms, and lyrics. Uh, it gives kids who don't love math or sports a chance to feel successful too. I think that's really important for confidence. Of course, not everyone will become a musician, and some students might not enjoy it at first. But even then, I think they'd learn to appreciate it and understand other cultures better. So I believe every child should have at least a basic music class each week.
speaking.translation: 有些人认为音乐教育应该成为学校课程的必修部分。你同意还是不同意这个观点？请解释你的理由。

content.stimulusText: Your professor is teaching an art history class. Write a post responding to the professor's question. Express and support your opinion. Make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words. Today we'll discuss the dynamic role of art in society. Clearly, art can be a powerful form of expression and communication that can challenge societal norms and help society progress. On the other hand, some people believe that art primarily serves as a way to preserve both the history and heritage of a people, a country, or even a civilization. Which do you believe plays a larger role?
content.post: Paul: I believe that art's role in preserving heritage is its most important role. As the world becomes more globalized, different cultures are losing their identities because they have been forced to adapt to the modern world. The arts have the power to prevent languages from being lost, can preserve important cultural traditions, and remind us of what makes us unique.

writing.answer:
I believe art's role in preserving heritage is slightly more important today, although challenging social norms remains essential. Paul is right that globalization can weaken languages, crafts, music, and stories. Recordings of traditional songs or exhibitions of regional art do more than display attractive objects; they preserve knowledge and identity that may disappear when younger generations move away.

Claire correctly argues that art can also challenge accepted ideas. Protest murals, experimental theater, and digital installations can expose injustice or help audiences imagine different social arrangements. However, even this critical function often depends on cultural memory. Artists reinterpret symbols precisely because communities understand what those symbols once meant.

Preservation should not turn art into an untouchable museum object. Living traditions survive when artists adapt them to new materials and concerns. By keeping a connection to the past while allowing reinterpretation, art gives society both a shared foundation and a language for change. For that reason, preserving heritage plays the larger role.

Dr. Gupta：今天我们将讨论艺术在社会中的动态作用。显然，艺术可以是一种强大的表达和交流形式，可以挑战社会规范并帮助社会进步。另一方面，有些人认为艺术主要作为一种方式来保存一个民族、一个国家甚至一个文明的历史和遗产。你认为哪个扮演更重要的角色？

Claire：我认为艺术可以通过呈现对传统思维的不同视角来挑战社会规范。例如，抽象艺术常常引发对既定规范和深层信念的批判性思考。通过这样做，它鼓励观众对新可能性敞开心扉，并促成改变。

Paul：我认为艺术在保护遗产方面的作用是其最重要的作用。随着世界变得更加全球化，不同文化因为被迫适应现代世界而正在失去其身份。艺术有能力防止语言消失，可以保存重要的文化传统，并提醒我们是什么让我们独一无二。

content.promptText: It's great to have you here. I'm interested in learning about your experiences with history education. First, what is one aspect of history that you find particularly interesting?

speaking.answer: One thing I find really interesting is how ordinary people lived in the past. I mean, textbooks talk a lot about kings and wars, but I'm curious about what a regular family ate, how children went to school, or what a town looked like on a normal day. Last year I read a book about daily life in ancient Rome, and, um, it was fascinating. People worried about prices, argued with neighbors, and joked in the streets, just like us. That made history feel human instead of distant. I think I enjoy this aspect because it helps me relate to people from the past. It reminds me that, despite all the changes, people have always wanted similar things, like safety, family, and a bit of fun.

content.promptText: Fascinating. Now think about when you studied history in school. What was a history-related activity or project you enjoyed, and what made it engaging for you?

speaking.answer: In high school, we did a project where each student interviewed an older relative about their life and then presented it to the class. I chose my grandfather. He told me stories about growing up in a small village and moving to the city for work. Uh, I recorded him, and I made a timeline with old photos. It was engaging because it was personal. I was hearing history directly from someone I love, instead of memorizing dates. Also, we all got to learn about each other's families, which made the class closer. I remember feeling proud when I presented, and my grandfather came to watch. That project made me realize that history is all around us, in the people we know.

content.promptText: That's interesting. Some people enjoy visiting historical sites. If you were to visit a historical site you've never before visited, which one would you choose, and why?

speaking.answer: If I could pick any place, I'd visit Machu Picchu in Peru. I've seen pictures many times, and I can't believe people built a city on top of a mountain so long ago. Honestly, I'd love to understand how they did it without modern machines. Um, I'd also like to hear the stories of the people who lived there and what their daily life looked like. Standing in a place like that, with clouds below you, must feel completely different from reading a book. Of course, I'd need to save money and plan a long trip. I'd probably go with my best friend, since she loves old places too. But I think the hiking, the views, and the history together would make it unforgettable. content.promptText: Good insights. History education is often debated in terms of its relevance in modern curriculums. Do you think the study of history remains important in today's educational system? Why or why not?

speaking.answer: I definitely think history remains important in today's educational system. Hmm, modern technology and current events make more sense when students understand what came before them. History can show how decisions about migration, laws, conflicts, or public health affected real people over time. It also teaches students to question sources instead of accepting every claim immediately, especially when information spreads quickly online. I mean, studying history shouldn't only mean memorizing names and dates; teachers should connect it to questions students still face today. Some details may seem distant, but the habits of comparing evidence and considering different perspectives are useful in any field. That is why I think history deserves a serious place in school.

writing.answer:
Dear Ms. Blake,

I visited Art Haven last weekend and wanted to share some feedback. I especially liked the local photography room on the second floor. The photos of the river market felt close to daily life here, and the short notes under each picture helped me see when and where they were taken.

I also hope the gallery can tell visitors more about the artists. Without that background, it is hard to know why a photographer chose a subject or what the project means, so the visit is less memorable than it could be.

Sincerely,
Lin

We've been discussing what factors people consider most important when choosing a career field. Some career counselors believe that financial considerations, such as high salaries and job security, are the primary factors that influence people's career decisions. Others argue that non-financial factors, like personal fulfillment, work-life balance, and opportunities to help others, are more important for long-term career satisfaction. Which factors do you think are more important when choosing a career field?
content.post: Kelly: I think non-financial factors are more important for choosing a career field because they determine long-term happiness and life satisfaction. When people choose careers based on personal interests, work-life balance, and opportunities to make meaningful contributions to society, they feel more motivated and engaged daily. Money feels empty if the work itself is boring, stressful, or conflicts with personal values.

writing.answer:
Kelly's point about long-term satisfaction is the one I would follow when choosing a career. Interest, balance, and a sense that the work helps someone keep people in a field after the novelty wears off. Paychecks matter, but they do not repair a job that drains people every Monday morning.

Andrew is not wrong about rent and family support. Ignoring income is reckless, especially for graduates who already carry loans. The mistake is treating salary as the only filter. Plenty of stable jobs pay enough to live on; far fewer keep people engaged for a decade.

My cousin took a lower-paid job at a city clinic instead of a higher-paying sales role. The hours are long, yet she still talks about patients by name and has stayed three years. A roommate who chased only bonuses left finance after eight months. That contrast is why I put non-financial factors first, while still requiring a basic income floor before anything else.

Dr. Diaz：我们一直在讨论人们选择职业领域时最看重哪些因素。一些职业顾问认为，经济因素，如高薪和工作保障，是影响人们职业决策的主要因素。另一些人则认为，非经济因素，如个人成就感、工作与生活的平衡以及帮助他人的机会，对于长期的职业满意度更为重要。在选择职业领域时，你认为哪些因素更重要？

Andrew：我认为经济因素在选择职业领域时是最重要的。高薪和工作保障为养家糊口和未来储蓄提供了稳定性。虽然个人成就感很有价值，但人们需要足够的收入来满足基本需求并实现经济独立，然后才能专注于职业满意度的其他方面。

Kelly：我认为非经济因素对于选择职业领域更为重要，因为它们决定了长期的幸福和生活满意度。当人们根据个人兴趣、工作与生活的平衡以及对社会做出有意义贡献的机会来选择职业时，他们每天都会感到更有动力和投入。如果工作本身枯燥、有压力或与个人价值观冲突，金钱会显得空洞。

speaking.answer: I think hobbies like gaming, cooking, and working out are especially popular right now among people my age. Gaming is easy to start, since many people already have a phone or computer, and you can play with friends who live far away. Um, cooking has become popular because there are so many short videos with simple recipes, and it's a nice way to save money too. Working out is popular because people are more aware of their health and want to relieve stress. Honestly, I also think people want hobbies that are fun but not too expensive or complicated.

speaking.answer: I think they play a huge role. Often, people don't start a hobby by themselves, they get introduced to it. Friends are also powerful, because if your friend invites you to join a hiking group, it's easier to say yes. Um, it feels less scary when you have someone to start with. content.promptText: Noted. Now many people start hobbies but don't continue with them. What do you think leads people to give up on their hobbies?

speaking.answer: I think the main reason is lack of time. Life gets busy with school, work, and family duties, and a hobby is usually the first thing people drop. Another reason is that progress can feel slow. For example, I tried learning the guitar, and after two months my fingers hurt and I still couldn't play a full song, so I stopped. Um, I think that's really common among beginners. People expect quick results, and when they don't see them, they lose motivation quickly. Cost can matter too, because equipment or classes may be expensive. Also, when no one around you shares the interest, it's lonely and easy to quit. So I'd say time, patience, and support are the big factors, honestly.

content.post: Andrew: Personally, I think the most crucial action people can take to help the environment is to recycle and reuse materials instead of throwing them away in the trash. By minimizing the amount of waste they create, individuals can significantly reduce their environmental footprint and conserve natural resources.

writing.answer:
Last week I counted six chargers still glowing in an empty study room after midnight. That small waste is why I side with Claire: unplugging unused devices is the daily habit most likely to cut environmental harm among the options we were given.

The effect is immediate. When a laptop, phone dock, or microwave stays plugged in, it keeps drawing power. Multiply that across a dorm floor, and the building burns electricity for no work at all. Walk or bike when you can, yes, but many people still need a car some days; unplugging works every evening without changing a commute plan.

Andrew wants more recycling and reuse. Those habits help, yet they depend on sorting rules, truck routes, and whether a plant will even accept the material. A power strip switched off does not wait for that chain. If each floor captain checked outlets once a night, our hall would waste less energy before the next recycling truck ever arrived. That is the action I would push first.

posts.name: Claire
posts.text: I believe reducing energy use is the most important thing we can do to protect the environment. If each person consumes a little bit less energy every day by unplugging devices, the result will be lower carbon emissions overall. And reducing carbon emissions helps combat climate change.
posts.textZh: 我相信减少能源使用是我们保护环境能做的最重要的事情。如果每个人每天通过拔掉设备插头来少消耗一点能源，结果将是整体碳排放量降低。而减少碳排放有助于应对气候变化。

posts.name: Andrew
posts.text: Personally, I think the most crucial action people can take to help the environment is to recycle and reuse materials instead of throwing them away in the trash. By minimizing the amount of waste they create, individuals can significantly reduce their environmental footprint and conserve natural resources.
posts.textZh: 就个人而言，我认为人们能为环境做的最关键行动是回收和再利用材料，而不是把它们扔进垃圾桶。通过减少他们产生的废物量，个人可以显著减少他们的环境足迹并节约自然资源。

speaking.prompt: Thank you for taking the time to speak with us today. I'd like to ask you some questions about your experiences with recycling and waste management. First, do you regularly recycle items such as paper, plastic, and glass? Why or why not?

content.promptText: Thank you for taking the time to speak with us today. I'd like to ask you some questions about your experiences with recycling and waste management. First, do you regularly recycle items such as paper, plastic, and glass? Why or why not?

speaking.answer: Yes, I recycle regularly. In my building, there are separate bins for paper, plastic, and glass, so it's very easy and quick to do. I usually rinse bottles and flatten boxes before I put them in the bins. My roommate and I remind each other when we forget. Um, I started doing this when my teacher showed us how much waste ends up in landfills, and that really stuck with me. I also use the recycling stations near the cafeteria. I also feel that if everyone does a little, it adds up to something big. Plus, recycling saves materials, so we don't need to take as many new resources from nature. Honestly, it takes only a minute or two a day, so I can't think of a good reason not to do it. It just feels like the responsible thing to do.
speaking.translation: 感谢您今天抽出时间与我们交谈。我想问您一些关于您在回收和废物处理方面的经历。首先，您是否经常回收纸张、塑料和玻璃等物品？为什么回收或不回收？

content.promptText: Thanks. Can you describe the recycling practices in your household or community?

speaking.answer: In my household, we keep a small container in the kitchen for recyclable items, and we empty it every few days. Hmm, we rinse bottles and cans first, because dirty containers can make the whole bin unpleasant. In my community, there are separate bins for paper, plastic, and general waste, although the signs could be clearer. Some neighbors also collect cardboard boxes from deliveries and flatten them before recycling. I think those practices work best when everyone understands the rules. I mean, people are willing to participate if the system is simple and the bins are nearby. Honestly, regular reminders from the building manager would probably help more residents recycle correctly.

speaking.prompt: Great, that's helpful. What challenges or difficulties do you face when trying to recycle? And how do you overcome them?

content.promptText: Great, that's helpful. What challenges or difficulties do you face when trying to recycle? And how do you overcome them?

speaking.answer: The main difficulty I face when recycling is figuring out what can actually be recycled. Uh, some packages look like plastic but include foil, paper, or food residue, and the instructions are not always easy to understand. Another problem is that the bins can be full or far away when I am carrying several items. To deal with that, I keep a small bag at home and take it out when I am already leaving for class or shopping. I also look up local rules when I have time, especially for electronics or batteries. Honestly, better labels would solve many problems. Clear information makes recycling much easier than asking people to guess.

speaking.prompt: Some people believe that effective recycling programs are crucial for reducing pollution and conserving natural resources, and therefore should be mandatory. Do you agree or disagree with this belief? Why or why not?
speaking.promptZh: 有些人认为有效的回收计划对于减少污染和保护自然资源至关重要，因此应该是强制性的。您是否同意或不同意这一观点？为什么？

content.promptText: Some people believe that effective recycling programs are crucial for reducing pollution and conserving natural resources, and therefore should be mandatory. Do you agree or disagree with this belief? Why or why not?

speaking.answer: I agree, mostly. Recycling really does reduce pollution and save resources, but when it's only optional, many people just don't bother, you know. Making it mandatory would give everyone the same rules and create a habit. A good example is a city that charges a fee for mixed garbage, and then people sort their trash more carefully. Um, I also think the government must make it easy, with clear instructions and enough bins, otherwise people will feel frustrated. And it shouldn't be too strict at the start, maybe warnings before fines. Still, I think the benefits are bigger than the inconvenience, because a cleaner environment helps everyone. So yes, I'd support mandatory recycling with good education and support for families.
speaking.translation: 有些人认为有效的回收计划对于减少污染和保护自然资源至关重要，因此应该是强制性的。您是否同意或不同意这一观点？为什么？

content.promptText: Your professor is teaching a class on urban planning. Write a post responding to the professor's question.
content.stimulusText: Your professor is teaching a class on urban planning. Write a post responding to the professor's question. Express and support your opinion. Make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words. We've been discussing strategies for managing urban growth. One approach is to focus on expanding public transportation to reduce traffic congestion and pollution. Another approach is to create more green spaces like parks and gardens to improve residents' quality of life. Which strategy do you think is more effective in managing urban growth? Why?
content.post: Paul: I think creating green spaces is the best response to the harmful side-effects of urban growth. Parks and gardens make urban areas more attractive and livable. My town is currently renovating its park system. Not only are green spaces more attractive than busy streets and sidewalks, they are more interesting and pleasant, too.

writing.answer:
Parks make a city nicer, and Paul is right that green space softens hard streets. For managing growth itself, though, I would expand public transportation first, as Kelly argues.

Growth means more people moving between home, school, and work every day. If that movement stays locked in cars, new parks sit beside louder roads and worse air. Buses and trains cut the number of trips that create congestion in the first place, which is the problem cities feel as they expand.

Kelly's town example matches what I see here. After a frequent bus corridor opened toward the east campus, weekend traffic near the stadium eased enough that weekend classes started on time again. The pocket park added the same year was pleasant for lunch, but it did not shorten anyone's drive. Build transit for daily movement, then place parks where riders already walk. That order handles growth more honestly than greenery alone, and it leaves room for both goals instead of treating parks as a substitute for mobility.

Kelly：我认为扩大公共交通是最有效的方法。它减少了不断发展的城市和社区的交通拥堵，并为居民提供了方便的出行方式。例如，在我的城镇，很容易乘坐公共汽车或电车去购物和文化活动，而且价格实惠。

Paul：我认为创造绿色空间是应对城市增长有害副作用的最佳方式。公园和花园使城市地区更具吸引力和宜居性。我的城镇目前正在翻新其公园系统。绿色空间不仅比繁忙的街道和人行道更具吸引力，而且更有趣、更宜人。

posts.text: I believe expanding public transportation is the most effective approach. speaking.answer: Well, my friends and family enjoy quite different things. My dad loves fishing, and he goes to the river almost every weekend. Um, my mom likes gardening, so our balcony is full of flowers. Among my friends, a lot of them play video games or basketball, and one of my close friends is really into photography. Also, hobbies bring people together, like when my friends and I play basketball after school. They give you something to look forward to, and I'd say that makes life feel more balanced and happy.

content.promptText: Great, that's helpful. Next, do you think hobbies should mostly be relaxing, or is it better if they challenge you? Why?

speaking.answer: I think hobbies should be mostly relaxing, but they should include a little challenge too. Uh, if a hobby is completely effortless, it can become passive entertainment rather than something that feels satisfying. On the other hand, if it is stressful all the time, people may stop doing it after a busy week. For me, the best hobbies let you focus and forget other worries while still learning something new, like improving a recipe or practicing a difficult song. I mean, progress is rewarding when it happens gradually. Honestly, the right balance depends on the person: some people relax through exercise or competition, while others prefer quiet activities like painting or reading.

speaking.answer: I think it is important for people to keep exploring new hobbies as they grow older. Hmm, trying something unfamiliar can keep daily life interesting and help people stay curious when their routines become fixed. New hobbies can also create friendships, especially after someone moves, retires, or begins a different stage of life. They do not need to become experts; even a short course or a weekend activity can reveal what someone enjoys. I mean, learning new things reminds people that they can still improve and adapt. Honestly, it is easy to assume that hobbies belong only to young people, but curiosity is valuable at every age. Exploring something new can make life feel larger.

Dear Ms. Turner,

I suggest posting a short pick-up and drop-off checklist at the counter and confirming the return steps by text before customers leave the lot. That would make the process clearer and faster. Thank you for considering this feedback.

Sincerely,
Lin

Supporters of online learning believe that it offers flexibility and access to a wide range of courses. Critics, on the other hand, believe that online learning lacks the personal interaction and structure of traditional classrooms. In your opinion, which of these factors do you believe plays a larger role in the effectiveness of online learning? Why?
content.post: Paul: I believe that the lack of personal interaction during online learning sessions can be detrimental to true learning. Traditional classrooms provide direct and immediate support from teachers that students don't receive during online learning classes. A classroom teacher can respond to students and answer questions in real time, which is not always possible when taking online classes.

writing.answer:
Paul's worry about missing real-time help in online classes is fair. I have sat through a confusing lecture video with no way to raise a hand. Even so, flexibility and access still decide whether online learning works for most students.

If the course does not exist where you live, interaction in a classroom never becomes an option. Claire is right that location is often the first wall. Online sections remove that wall and let people take specialized classes that their local campus never offers, including night workers who cannot sit in a daytime lecture hall.

The better designs keep access and add contact points. When my required methods course filled on campus, the online section still had weekly live office hours and small breakout groups. I finished on schedule and got answers within the same week. Interaction matters, but it only helps after a student can enroll. That is why I treat flexibility as the larger factor in online learning's effectiveness.

content.promptText: Thanks for joining the study. First, do you mainly gain historical knowledge from school classes or from independent reading outside class?

speaking.answer: I mainly learn history from school classes, um, but I also do some independent reading when a topic really catches me. In class, teachers give a clear timeline and explain causes, which helps me understand the big picture instead of random facts. Outside class, I sometimes read short articles or watch documentaries about periods we already covered in lectures. Honestly, those extras make the topic feel more alive, especially when they include personal stories from ordinary people. Still, without the classroom structure, I would probably miss important connections. So school is my main source, and independent reading is more like a useful supplement when I want deeper details.

speaking.prompt: When studying history, which area interests you more: culture, politics, or another topic?

content.promptText: When studying history, which area interests you more: culture, politics, or another topic?

speaking.answer: For me, it's culture, definitely. I find daily life in the past more interesting than wars and governments. Like, what did ordinary people eat, wear, or believe? Uh, I once read about how families in ancient cities celebrated their festivals, and I loved how some traditions still look similar today. Culture also helps me understand why people in different countries behave the way they do today. Politics can be important, of course, and it explains major events. But sometimes it kind of feels like a list of names and dates, which I find really hard to remember. Culture feels more human to me, with stories, art, food, and music. That's why, when I study history, I always pay the most attention to cultural topics.
speaking.translation: 在学习历史时，你更感兴趣哪个领域：文化、政治还是其他主题？

context.text: You are participating in a research interview with me about how people study history. I will ask you some questions. From this point on, the questions will not appear on screen, so please listen carefully.

speaking.prompt: Have you visited a museum? Can places like museums deepen your understanding of history?

content.promptText: Have you visited a museum? Can places like museums deepen your understanding of history?

speaking.answer: Yes, I've visited a local history museum with my class, and it did deepen my understanding a lot. Seeing real objects, like tools, clothing, and handwritten letters, made the period feel concrete instead of abstract. Um, in textbooks I can memorize dates, but in a museum I notice small details that show how hard daily life was. The exhibits also included short audio explanations, which helped me connect objects to larger historical events. Honestly, after that visit I remembered the material much better during exams. So I think museums can deepen understanding because they turn history into something you can see and almost touch, not only something you read about.

content.promptText: Do you agree that studying history can help people avoid repeating past mistakes? Why or why not?

speaking.answer: I agree to some extent. History gives us examples of what went wrong, like economic crises or wars that started from misunderstandings. If leaders and citizens study them, they can notice similar warning signs and act earlier. Um, a simple example is how countries learned to cooperate more after major wars, hoping to prevent another one. But I also think people don't always learn, even when the lessons are clear. Sometimes they ignore history because of pride or short-term interests. And every situation is a little different, so old solutions don't always fit. So, studying history helps, you know, but it's not a guarantee. It gives us a better chance of avoiding mistakes, but only if we really pay attention.

To: Ms. Garcia

writing.answer:
Dear Ms. Garcia,

I recently had dinner at your restaurant with two classmates, and overall I enjoyed the experience. The atmosphere was comfortable, and the main dishes were fresh and well prepared.

However, a few parts of the service were disappointing. We waited a long time before anyone came to take our order, and it was difficult to get a server's attention when we needed water and extra plates. Also, one side dish arrived cold, so one of my classmates could not enjoy it properly.

I hope the restaurant can add more staff during busy hours and ask servers to check on each table more regularly. It would also help to review orders before they leave the kitchen. These changes would make the dining experience much smoother.

Sincerely,
Ruide

content.post: Claire: While literature has some impact, other forms of media like television and social media are more influential in shaping societal values today. These platforms reach a broader audience and can quickly spread ideas and trends. Most people prefer these newer forms of media because they are less challenging than literary works are.

writing.answer:
Claire is right that television and social media move ideas faster than novels do. Speed is not the same as lasting influence, though, so I still think literature plays a significant role in shaping societal values.

A feed can make a slogan famous by evening. A novel or play asks readers to stay with one character's choices for hours, which is how people practice judging fairness, loyalty, or cruelty without a timer. Andrew's point about empathy fits that slower process, and history shows books feeding reform movements long before a clip can trend.

I saw the difference in a first-year seminar. Students shared viral clips about housing costs during the first week, then spent a month on a novel about tenants and landlords. The clips started the anger; the book gave them the language they kept using in later debates. Media can spark attention, but literature still trains the deeper judgments people carry into adult life. That lasting work is why its role remains significant.

Dr. Diaz：我们一直在讨论文学在塑造社会价值观中的作用。文学，包括戏剧、诗歌和小说，可以反映并影响一个社会的信仰和行为。有些人认为文学是激发积极社会变革的有力工具。但批评者认为，与其他媒体形式相比，文学的影响有限。你认为文学在塑造社会价值观方面是否起着重要作用？为什么？

Andrew：文学在塑造社会价值观方面起着重要作用，因为它给人们提供了感知和思考他人感受的独特机会。通过讲故事，它可以激发同理心，引发对社会问题的批判性思考。书籍在历史上影响了运动，并提高了对重要事业的认识。

Claire：虽然文学有一定影响，但如今电视和社交媒体等其他媒体形式在塑造社会价值观方面更具影响力。这些平台覆盖更广泛的受众，能迅速传播思想和趋势。大多数人更喜欢这些新媒体形式，因为它们比文学作品更容易理解。

posts.text: While literature has some impact, other forms of media like television and social media are more influential in shaping societal values today. These platforms reach a broader audience and can quickly spread ideas and trends. Most people prefer these newer forms of media because they are less challenging than literary works are.
posts.textZh: 虽然文学有一定影响，但如今电视和社交媒体等其他媒体形式在塑造社会价值观方面更具影响力。这些平台覆盖更广泛的受众，能迅速传播思想和趋势。大多数人更喜欢这些新媒体形式，因为它们比文学作品更容易理解。

speaking.prompt: Thanks for your time. I'd like to ask you some questions about gift-giving habits. First, do you like to give gifts? Why?
speaking.promptZh: 感谢你的时间。我想问你一些关于送礼习惯的问题。首先，你喜欢送礼物吗？为什么？

content.promptText: Thanks for your time. I'd like to ask you some questions about gift-giving habits. First, do you like to give gifts? Why?

speaking.answer: Yes, I love giving gifts, honestly. It makes me happy to see someone's face light up when they open something that I picked carefully. I enjoy thinking about what the person likes, like their hobbies or favorite colors, and then finding something that fits. I usually write a short card by hand too, because I think words matter. Last month, I gave my roommate a small, cute notebook with her name on it, and, um, she was so touched that she almost cried. That moment felt even better to me than receiving a gift myself, I think. Giving gifts also shows people that I'm paying attention to them, and it makes our relationship stronger. It doesn't have to be expensive. A thoughtful little gift can mean much more than a costly one, in my opinion.
speaking.translation: 感谢你的时间。我想问你一些关于送礼习惯的问题。首先，你喜欢送礼物吗？为什么？

context.text: You have volunteered for a research study about gift-giving habits and culture. You will have a short online interview with me. I will ask you some questions. From this point on, the questions will not appear on screen, so please listen carefully.

speaking.prompt: Thank you. What are the factors that you consider when giving gifts to other people?

content.promptText: Thank you. What are the factors that you consider when giving gifts to other people?

speaking.answer: I think about a few things. The first one is the person's interests, because a gift is only special if they'll actually use it or enjoy it. For example, my friend loves photography, so I once gave her a small lens cleaning kit, and she was thrilled. Second, um, I consider my budget. I'm a student, so I can't spend a lot, but I try to add something personal, like a short handwritten card. Third is the occasion, of course. A birthday gift is different from a thank-you gift, you know. Finally, I think about timing and wrapping, since a nice presentation shows care. If I keep all these in mind, the gift usually feels thoughtful and the person feels truly appreciated.
speaking.translation: 谢谢。在给别人送礼时，你会考虑哪些因素？

context.text: You have volunteered for a research study about gift-giving habits and culture. You will have a short online interview with me. I will ask you some questions. From this point on, the questions will not appear on screen, so please listen carefully.

speaking.prompt: I see. What is one memorable gift you have received, or that you gave to others before?

content.promptText: I see. What is one memorable gift you have received, or that you gave to others before?

speaking.answer: One gift I'll never forget is a scrapbook that my best friend made for my eighteenth birthday party. She collected photos from our years together, tickets from movies we watched, and even some little notes from my classmates. She even stayed up until midnight to finish the last pages, and she knows my whole story because we've been friends since middle school. Honestly, when I opened it, uh, I got really emotional, because I could see how much time and effort she spent on it. It wasn't expensive at all, but it was full of memories, so it meant more to me than any fancy present. I still keep it on my bookshelf at home, and I flip through it whenever I'm feeling down or missing her. That experience taught me that the best gifts come from the heart, not from the price tag.
speaking.translation: 我明白了。你收到过，或者送给别人过，什么印象深刻的礼物？

context.text: You have volunteered for a research study about gift-giving habits and culture. You will have a short online interview with me. I will ask you some questions. From this point on, the questions will not appear on screen, so please listen carefully.

content.promptText: Great. Last question. Do you prefer to make a wish list and let other people send you gifts on the list, or do you prefer to have surprises?

speaking.answer: I prefer a short wish list more than pure surprises. A list helps people choose something I will actually use, and it reduces awkward gifts that sit unused. Uh, I still like a little surprise inside that list, like which item they pick or how they wrap it. Complete surprises can be fun, but sometimes they miss my taste or size completely. I mean, receiving a thoughtful listed gift feels better than pretending to like something random. At the same time, I don't want a huge catalog that removes all creativity. So a small wish list with room for personal choice is my favorite balance.
speaking.translation: 很好。最后一个问题。你更喜欢列一个心愿清单让别人按清单送你礼物，还是更喜欢惊喜？

content.email:
To: John
Subject: Invitation to Join a New Project

writing.answer:
Dear John,

I am writing to invite you to join a new project that our team will begin next month. The project focuses on improving our online customer feedback system, and I think it would be a great opportunity for you.

I believe you would be a valuable member of the team because you are careful, organized, and good at solving technical problems. Your recent work on the database update showed that you can handle detailed tasks under pressure, and this project will need exactly those skills.

Please let me know if you are interested in participating. If so, we can meet later this week to discuss the goals, schedule, and your possible responsibilities in more detail.

Best,
Ruide

content.post: Paul: I disagree with Claire. Social well-being should take priority. For instance, improving access to education would help to create a more informed citizenry and produce more individuals capable of innovating and helping humankind to progress.

writing.answer:
When spring floods closed two clinics near the river last year, patients missed appointments for weeks. That is why I agree with Claire that environmental conservation should lead when we talk about securing the future.

Paul wants education, equality, and health care to come first, and those goals matter. They also need physical conditions that stay stable. Dirty water, failed crops, and repeated floods interrupt schools and hospitals no matter how good the policy paper looks on paper.

Protecting wetlands, forests, and clean waterways is not a side hobby. It keeps the ground under social programs from washing away. Conservation can also serve people directly: the restored marsh outside my city now holds stormwater that used to enter ground floors, so fewer families lose workdays to cleanup. Put environmental protection in the lead, and keep social investment close behind, not as a substitute that assumes the planet will wait while we catch up later. Without that order, progress keeps rebuilding after the next storm.

content.promptText: Thanks for joining today's interview. I'd like to ask you a few questions about spending habits. First, when you buy products, do you tend to make impulse purchases, or do you carefully plan what to buy?

speaking.answer: I'd say I'm a planner for big purchases, but I'm a bit impulsive with small ones. For example, if I need a laptop or a coat, I research for days, read reviews, and compare prices at different stores. Um, but when I'm in a supermarket and I see a new snack or a cute notebook near the checkout, I often just grab it. Last week I bought three pens I didn't even need. Those little purchases add up, and at the end of the month I wonder where my money went. So I'm trying to improve. I make a list before I shop, and I try to stick to it. Honestly, it works pretty well when I'm not hungry. So overall, I'd call myself a careful person with an occasional weakness for small treats.
speaking.translation: 感谢参加今天的访谈。我想问你一些关于消费习惯的问题。首先，当你购买产品时，你倾向于冲动购物，还是仔细计划要买什么？

content.promptText: Great. Now let me ask about budgeting. Some people set a weekly or monthly budget, and others do not. What is your approach to managing expenses?

speaking.answer: I set a monthly budget, because a weekly one feels too tight for me. At the beginning of the month, I figure out my fixed costs, like rent and phone, and then I decide how much to spend on food and fun. Uh, I keep track using a simple app that shows me where my money goes, and the charts really help. If I notice I'm spending too much on takeout, I cut back for a while. Last month it was bubble tea, so I switched to making it at home. And I review the numbers every Sunday night. I also set aside a small amount for savings the moment I get paid, so I don't spend it by accident. I mean, it's like paying myself first. Honestly, this system isn't complicated, but it keeps me calm and prevents unpleasant surprises.
speaking.translation: 很好。现在我想问问预算方面。有些人会制定每周或每月的预算，有些人则不会。你管理开支的方式是什么？

content.promptText: Interesting to hear your thoughts. When making an expensive purchase, some people prefer to wait and save up their money, while others prefer to have the item right away and pay for it over time. Which do you prefer, and why?

speaking.answer: I prefer to save up and wait. Paying over time sounds easy, but you often end up paying extra interest, and I don't like owing money. I also think waiting makes me value the item more. Um, last year I wanted a new tablet, and I could have bought it with a payment plan right away. Instead, I saved for four months, and when I finally bought it, I felt proud and I took better care of it. Waiting also gave me time to decide whether I really needed it. Of course, if something is an emergency, like a broken laptop I need for school, paying in installments might make sense. But for normal wants, I'd choose patience, since it keeps me out of debt.

content.promptText: Lastly, some people believe it is important to save as much money as possible for the future, while others feel it is better to spend more freely on things that bring satisfaction. What is your opinion, and why?

speaking.answer: I think a balanced approach is best, but I lean toward saving first. Having emergency money reduces anxiety when unexpected costs appear, like medical bills or sudden travel. Uh, if every dollar is already spent, small problems become large crises. At the same time, I do not believe people should never spend on enjoyment. After I set aside savings and cover necessary costs, I allow a limited amount for meals with friends or hobbies. Honestly, that spending keeps life from feeling only about restriction. Extreme saving can also create stress if it removes all pleasure. So my opinion is save enough for security first, then spend thoughtfully on things that truly bring satisfaction.

Some people believe endangered animals should be protected in environments with little or no human activity, so they can live and reproduce without disturbance. Which approach do you think is more effective for protecting wildlife? Why?
content.post: Kelly: I think eco-friendly farming and consumer choices are more practical. Humans already use a lot of land, so making farms and products less harmful can protect wildlife while still supporting people's needs.

writing.answer:
I think protected habitats are the most effective foundation for wildlife conservation, although eco-friendly farming should reinforce them. Paul is right that endangered species need places where they can feed, breed, and migrate without constant noise, roads, or construction. A protected wetland, for example, can preserve nesting areas for birds that would disappear if every parcel were developed.

Kelly's approach is also necessary because animals do not recognize park boundaries. Pesticides used on nearby farms can poison rivers inside a reserve, while fences can block migration routes. Governments should therefore support farmers who reduce chemicals, preserve hedges, and create wildlife corridors connecting larger protected areas.

Still, consumer choices and voluntary farming changes are often inconsistent. Legally protected habitat provides an immediate refuge and a clear standard that can be monitored. The strongest policy is to secure large, connected reserves first, then make surrounding farms and supply chains safer so wildlife can survive beyond those core areas.

speaking.answer: I'd say I get a bit of relaxation almost every day, but real long breaks only on weekends. During the week, I find small moments, like having tea after lunch for fifteen minutes or going for a short walk after dinner. speaking.answer: Most evenings, I like to play the guitar for about half an hour or so. It's definitely my favorite way to relax. I'm not a professional or anything, you know, I just play simple songs I like a lot, usually starting with one slow song and then trying something harder. content.promptText: Great. And lastly, some people see leisure time as a basic need for everyone, while others see it as a luxury that depends on personal circumstances. Which view do you agree with, and why?

speaking.answer: I agree that leisure is a basic need. Everyone needs rest, whatever their job or situation. Without it, people get exhausted, lose focus, and even get sick over time. I mean, think about workers with very long hours every week. If they never have time to relax, their health and their relationships suffer, and, um, their work gets worse too. Of course, how people spend leisure time can depend on money. Someone might travel abroad while another just takes a walk in a park. But the need to rest is the same for all of us. So I'd say leisure isn't a luxury. It's something societies should protect, for instance with reasonable work hours and free public parks and libraries.

Today in our economics class, we are discussing minimum wage laws, which require employers to pay workers at least a certain hourly rate. Supporters argue that these laws help reduce poverty and improve workers' quality of life. Critics, however, worry that higher wages may increase business costs and reduce job opportunities, especially for young or low-skilled workers. Do you believe minimum wage laws are good for the economy? Why or why not?
content.post: Claire: I disagree because minimum wage laws can hurt small businesses. If a restaurant must pay every worker more, it might raise prices, reduce hours, or hire fewer people. This could make it harder for inexperienced workers to find jobs.

writing.answer:
I believe well-designed minimum wage laws are good for the economy because they raise living standards without requiring every employer to make the same adjustment overnight. Paul is right that low-income workers usually spend additional earnings on necessities such as groceries, transportation, and rent, so much of that money returns quickly to local businesses.

Claire's concern is still important. A small restaurant with narrow profit margins might reduce hours if wages rise sharply in a single month. However, this problem can be limited by announcing increases years in advance and adjusting rates to regional living costs. Governments could also offer temporary payroll credits to very small firms during the transition.

In my view, eliminating wage standards would leave responsible employers competing against businesses that survive by underpaying workers. A gradual, predictable wage floor creates fairer competition, strengthens consumer demand, and gives companies enough time to improve productivity rather than suddenly cutting jobs.

Dr. Gupta：今天在我们的经济学课上，我们讨论最低工资法，该法要求雇主至少按一定的小时费率支付工人工资。支持者认为这些法律有助于减少贫困并改善工人的生活质量。然而，批评者担心更高的工资可能会增加企业成本并减少就业机会，尤其是对年轻或低技能工人而言。你认为最低工资法对经济有益吗？为什么？

Paul：我认为最低工资法通常对经济有益，因为它们赋予工人更多的消费能力。例如，如果低收入工人赚得更多，他们可能会购买更多的食品、衣物和服务，这有助于当地企业。公平的工资还可以减轻压力并提高工人的生产力。

Claire：我不同意，因为最低工资法可能会伤害小企业。如果一家餐厅必须给每位工人支付更多工资，它可能会提高价格、减少工时或减少雇佣人数。这可能会使缺乏经验的工人更难找到工作。

speaking.answer: First, I think about the person. What do they like, and what do they need right now? If my brother is starting a new job, for example, uh, a good notebook or a nice bag would be useful. Second, I consider the occasion. A birthday gift can be fun, but a wedding gift should be more formal. Third is my budget, because I'm a student and can't spend too much. I mean, a thoughtful gift doesn't have to be expensive anyway. I also ask their friends for hints if I'm really stuck. Finally, I try to add something personal, like a handwritten card. In my experience, a gift that shows you listened to the person is always better than something fancy but random.

speaking.prompt: I see. Describe a memorable gift you have given or received. What made it special?

content.promptText: I see. Describe a memorable gift you have given or received. What made it special?

speaking.answer: The most special gift I ever received was a scarf my grandmother knitted for me when I left home for college. It wasn't fancy, and the color was a little strange, honestly, but she'd made it by hand over several weeks. Um, she told me she worked on it every evening after dinner. When I put it on in the cold winter, I felt like she was right there with me. I've kept it all these years. Even now, I wear it on the coldest days every winter, and my friends always tell me how cozy it looks. What made it special was all the time and love she put into it. It's still my favorite thing in my closet. Every time I wear it, I remember her kind face and the way she smiled when she handed it to me.

speaking.prompt: Great. Some people think it is helpful to make online gift registries so others know exactly what to give, while others feel gifts should be a surprise. Which point of view do you agree with, and why?

content.promptText: Great. Some people think it is helpful to make online gift registries so others know exactly what to give, while others feel gifts should be a surprise. Which point of view do you agree with, and why?

speaking.answer: I prefer gifts to remain a surprise, especially among close friends and family. The guessing and personal choice are part of what makes giving meaningful. A carefully chosen novel, for example, shows that the giver understands my interests in a way that picking from a list may not. Uh, surprises also create memorable reactions and stories. However, registries are useful for weddings or expensive household items because they prevent duplicates and wasted money. In those situations, practicality matters more. For birthdays, though, I'd rather receive a small unexpected present, even if it's imperfect. Honestly, the thought behind it usually matters more to me than getting exactly what I requested.

This week, we're examining how social media affects people's daily social interactions and self-confidence. Some researchers suggest that social media can make people feel lonely and insecure because they constantly compare their lives to others' posts and receive negative comments from strangers. Others argue that social media helps people maintain friendships, find communities with shared interests, and receive encouragement from supportive networks. Which view is more accurate? Provide details to explain your choice.
content.post: Paul: I think social media can positively impact people's social connections and personal confidence when used thoughtfully. It allows people to maintain friendships across long distances, find communities with shared hobbies or interests, and receive encouragement during difficult times. Social media also gives shy individuals comfortable platforms to express themselves and build confidence through positive interactions with supportive online communities.

writing.answer:
I think the more accurate view is that social media can strengthen relationships and confidence when people use it thoughtfully, although the risks Kelly describes are real. Paul’s point is strong: social media helps friends stay connected across distance, and it can give shy people a lower-pressure way to join conversations and find communities with shared interests.

Kelly is right that constant comparison and harsh comments can damage self-confidence. Seeing only polished achievements can make ordinary life feel inadequate, and online conflict can push people toward shallow interactions. Those harms matter, especially for users who spend long hours scrolling without limits.

Still, the problem seems more about how the tools are used than about the tools themselves. If people follow supportive communities, limit comparison-driven content, and treat online contact as a supplement to offline friendship, social media can provide encouragement and belonging. For that reason, I side with the more positive view, while recognizing that uncritical use can clearly hurt social confidence.

Dr. Diaz：本周我们正在研究社交媒体如何影响人们的日常社交互动和自信心。一些研究人员认为，社交媒体会让人们感到孤独和不安全，因为他们不断将自己的生活与他人的帖子进行比较，并收到陌生人的负面评论。另一些人则认为，社交媒体帮助人们维持友谊，找到有共同兴趣的社区，并从支持性网络中获得鼓励。哪种观点更准确？请提供细节来解释你的选择。

Kelly：我认为社交媒体对人们的社交关系和自信心有显著的负面影响。当人们不断看到他人的度假照片、成就和完美时刻时，他们会对自己的生活和成就感到不足。此外，负面评论和在线争论会造成压力，使人们不愿表达真实意见，导致肤浅的互动而非有意义的友谊。

Paul：我认为，如果使用得当，社交媒体可以对人们的社交联系和个人信心产生积极影响。它允许人们维持远距离的友谊，找到有共同爱好或兴趣的社区，并在困难时期获得鼓励。社交媒体还为害羞的人提供了舒适的自我表达平台，并通过与支持性在线社区的积极互动建立信心。

content.promptText: Thanks for taking part in the study. Today I'd like to ask you a few questions about environmental awareness and lifestyle choices. First, what, if any, environmentally friendly practices, such as recycling, do you employ in your daily life?

speaking.answer: Yes, I do a few things. The easiest one is recycling, so I separate paper, plastic, and glass at home. Uh, I also bring my own reusable bag when I go shopping, and I carry a water bottle instead of buying plastic ones. Another habit is turning off lights and unplugging chargers when I leave a room, which saves electricity. I try to walk or take the bus rather than ask for a ride, too. speaking.answer: If I could make just one change, I'd stop using single-use plastic, like bags, straws, and bottles. content.promptText: Good points. Some people believe that individual actions alone are not enough to address environmental problems. Do you agree or disagree with this statement? Why?

speaking.answer: I agree, mostly. Individual actions matter, but they can't solve everything. Um, a single person recycling or using less water is helpful, but huge amounts of pollution come from factories, power plants, and transportation systems. Those need new rules and investments from governments and big companies, which no single person can provide. Still, I don't think individual actions are useless. They create awareness, and when many people change their habits, businesses and leaders notice. So I'd say we need both: people making better daily choices, and governments and companies making large changes. Without that combination, I honestly don't think we can fix problems like climate change.

However, in recent decades, the pace of scientific and technological progress has increased dramatically, with new discoveries and inventions being developed almost every day. Some people think that this rapid progress in science and technology is beneficial for society overall and should be encouraged. Others believe this progress is happening too quickly and could create serious problems. Which view do you agree with, and why?
content.post: Andrew: The fact that most people don't have a say in how these new inventions are implemented concerns me. Just think about the loss of jobs due to the automation of many kinds of work; this has become widespread during this time of rapid technological change. People who lose their jobs will probably not believe this type of progress is beneficial.

writing.answer:
I agree that rapid progress in science and technology is beneficial overall and should be encouraged, but society also needs stronger ways to manage its side effects. Claire’s medical example is convincing. Faster research has made many treatments cheaper and more widely available, and people facing serious illness clearly benefit when discovery moves quickly.

Andrew raises a real problem, though. When automation spreads faster than workers can retrain, people can lose jobs and feel excluded from decisions about new technology. That does not mean the progress itself is bad; it means the transition is uneven and often poorly managed.

In my view, the better response is not to slow discovery, but to pair it with education, worker support, and public discussion about how inventions are used. If society invests in those protections, rapid scientific progress can improve health, communication, and daily life while reducing the harm Andrew describes. For that reason, I support encouraging technological progress with stronger social safeguards.

content.promptText: Thank you. When learning about history, whether through school or on your own, what aspects do you find most intriguing: cultural, political, or something else?

speaking.answer: For me, the cultural side is the most intriguing. I really love learning about food, music, festivals, and traditions, and how they changed over time. Politics is important too, but, honestly, I find it a bit dry. Lists of treaties and elections don't stay in my head. Culture feels alive. For example, I once learned how a simple dish spread along trade routes and was changed by every country it reached. Um, I thought that was amazing, because one bowl of food told a story about travel, trade, and people mixing. I think culture shows how ordinary people lived and what they cared about. So when I study history on my own, I almost always follow the cultural path first.

speaking.prompt: I see. Have you ever visited a historical site or museum? Do you think visiting such a place enhances your understanding of history? Why or why not?

content.promptText: I see. Have you ever visited a historical site or museum? Do you think visiting such a place enhances your understanding of history? Why or why not?

speaking.answer: Yes, I visited the Nanjing Massacre Memorial Hall with my history class two years ago, and it really changed how I understood that period. Before the visit, I knew the dates and casualty figures from a textbook, but they felt distant. At the museum, I saw family photographs, letters, and everyday objects left by victims. Um, one small child's shoe affected me more than a page of statistics because it represented a real life interrupted by war. Our guide also explained how survivor testimony was collected and checked. The visit made history emotional, but it also showed me that careful evidence is essential when remembering painful events. So yes, museums can deepen understanding a lot.

speaking.prompt: Good points. Some people believe that studying history helps prevent repeating past mistakes. Do you agree or disagree with this idea? Why?

content.promptText: Good points. Some people believe that studying history helps prevent repeating past mistakes. Do you agree or disagree with this idea? Why?

speaking.answer: I mostly agree, though I'd say it's not automatic. If people actually study the past, they can recognize warning signs, like how economic crises or unfair policies led to big problems before. For example, learning about past financial crashes helps people see why careless borrowing is dangerous. Um, I think that's the real value of history. It gives us examples to learn from. But, you know, people don't always listen. Sometimes leaders ignore the lessons because they believe this time is different. So history can't guarantee that mistakes won't happen again. Still, knowing the past gives us a better chance of making good choices. That's why I agree that studying history is useful, as long as we really apply what we learn.

In today's communication class, we are discussing ways speakers can make their ideas effective. Some people believe speakers should use storytelling because vivid stories can hold the audience's attention and make ideas easier to remember. Others believe direct communication is better because it presents the main message clearly and efficiently. Which approach do you think is more effective in speeches? Why?
content.post: Claire: I prefer direct communication. In many situations, listeners mainly want the key information, so too many stories may distract them from the speaker's main point.

writing.answer:
I think the most effective speeches combine a direct central message with one carefully chosen story. Paul is right that listeners remember concrete experiences better than abstract claims. A public-health speaker, for example, can explain vaccination statistics and then describe one family whose child avoided serious illness. The story gives the numbers a human meaning.

Claire's warning is equally important. If a speaker tells several long stories before stating a position, the audience may remember interesting characters but forget the recommendation. Direct communication is especially necessary during emergencies, technical briefings, or meetings where listeners must act quickly.

A strong speaker should state the main point early, use a brief relevant story as evidence or illustration, and finish with a clear conclusion. This structure does not force a choice between emotion and efficiency. Storytelling secures attention and memory, while direct statements ensure that the audience understands exactly what the speaker believes and what action, if any, should follow.

content.promptText: Thank you. How important do you think social interactions are for maintaining a healthy lifestyle? Please explain why.

speaking.answer: I think it's very important. Humans are social by nature, and spending time with others makes us happier and less stressed. When I go through a hard week, talking with friends really helps me feel better, uh, even a short chat over coffee can change my mood. Social activity can also encourage healthy habits. For example, I exercise more when I have a friend to go running with, since we keep each other motivated. On the other hand, when people stay isolated for a long time, they can feel lonely or depressed, and that affects their sleep and appetite too. I mean, physical health and emotional health are connected. So I'd say good relationships are as important as eating well and getting enough exercise.

speaking.answer: Well, the biggest change I've noticed is how much of our communication has moved online. A few years ago, my friends and I would meet up almost every weekend. Now we often just chat in group messages or play online games together, especially since some of us live in different cities. I do miss those long lazy weekends together. Um, I think it's both good and bad. It's good because I can stay in touch with friends far away, and it's easy to share photos or plans instantly. But the downside is that face-to-face conversations are getting rarer, and sometimes at dinner everyone is looking at their phones. I mean, it feels less personal. So overall I'd say it's mixed, and we just need to make an effort to meet in person regularly.

content.promptText: Good points. Do you think online social platforms will eventually replace face-to-face interactions, or will personal interactions remain indispensable? Why do you think so?

speaking.answer: I do not think online platforms will fully replace face-to-face interaction. They are excellent for convenience when friends live far apart, but personal contact offers two things a screen cannot fully provide. First, body language is clearer in the same room. A pause, a smile, or a change in posture can show feelings that disappear in text. Uh, second, shared physical experiences create stronger memories. Cooking together or walking after class builds trust through action, not only through messages. Online tools will stay part of daily life, of course. Still, most people need real meetings for close relationships and important conversations. So personal interaction remains indispensable even as platforms keep growing.

content.post: Paul: I think an authoritative leadership style is often more effective. Clear direction from one person allows a team to make decisions quickly and avoid confusion. This approach can be especially helpful in high-pressure situations when there is little time for extended discussion.

writing.answer:
I think a collaborative leadership style is generally more effective in a business setting, although authoritative leadership can be useful in emergencies. Kelly makes a strong point that involving team members creates a greater sense of responsibility. When people help shape a decision, they are more likely to support it and work hard to carry it out. Collaboration can also bring in ideas that a single leader might miss, which improves the quality of the final plan.

Paul is right that clear direction is valuable when time is limited. In a crisis, a leader may need to decide quickly without long discussion. Even so, most daily business work is not an emergency. Over time, teams that only follow orders may become passive and less creative.

For that reason, I prefer collaborative leadership as the default approach. A good manager can still make firm decisions when needed, but regular input from the team usually produces better results and a stronger workplace culture.

Dr. Gupta：我们一直在讨论企业管理中不同的领导风格。有些领导者采用权威式方法：他们独立做出决定，并期望团队成员遵循他们的指示。其他领导者则更喜欢协作式方法：他们让团队成员参与决策，并鼓励反馈。你认为在商业环境中哪种领导风格更有效？为什么？

Kelly：我认为协作式领导风格更有效。让团队成员参与决策可以增强团队合作和责任感。员工也可能贡献有用的想法，这可以提高团队工作的质量和数量。

Paul：我认为权威式领导风格通常更有效。一个人给出明确的指示可以让团队快速做出决定，避免混乱。这种方法在压力大、时间紧的情况下尤其有用。

speaking.answer: One project that was really challenging was a group research paper on city traffic in my sophomore year. First, our team had four people with different schedules, so even finding a meeting time was hard. Second, uh, the data was messy, and we spent almost a week cleaning it before we could even start the analysis. Also, we disagreed about the main argument, which created some tension. Eventually we divided the work clearly and set weekly deadlines, and that made things smoother. In the end, we got a good grade, and our teacher praised the clear data charts. Honestly, the hardest part was communication, not the research itself, but I learned a lot about teamwork and about staying calm under pressure.

content.promptText: Noted. In your opinion, what is the most important skill students should develop during their education? Please provide reasons for your answer.

speaking.answer: I'd say critical thinking is the most important skill. It means asking questions and checking whether information is reliable instead of just accepting it. Nowadays, there's so much content online, and some of it is wrong or misleading, so students need to judge what's true. Um, it also really helps in everyday decisions, like choosing a major or managing money. For example, in one class, our teacher asked us to compare two articles on the same topic, and I realized that each one left out something important. That really changed how I read things online. Critical thinking makes learning deeper, you know, because you understand why something is true, not just memorize it. I believe it prepares students for almost any career they choose.

speaking.answer: I agree, mostly. Studying many subjects makes you a more complete person, I think. For example, I'm a science major, but I took a history class last year, and it helped me understand how societies and ideas changed over time. Um, it also improved my writing and discussion skills, which I now use in every course. Different subjects train your brain in different ways, so you become more flexible and creative. And honestly, students often don't know what career they'll end up in, so it's smart to keep your options open early on. Of course, too many unrelated classes could be a waste of time if there's no focus. But some variety is healthy, and it makes school more interesting, too.

To: Maya

writing.answer:
Dear Maya,

I wanted to follow up on the bookstore I mentioned in literature class. I first heard about it from a classmate who saw a flyer near the student center, and then I walked over after class last Thursday.

I usually look for contemporary fiction, essay collections, and a few poetry titles. If you are free this weekend, would you like to visit the bookstore with me? We could browse for an hour and then get coffee nearby.

Best,
Your classmate

As the job market evolves rapidly, schools face the challenge of preparing students for future careers. Some argue that high schools should have more flexibility in their curriculum to quickly adapt to these changes, ensuring that students gain relevant skills for job market trends. Others believe that a stable, consistent curriculum that ensures a basic, well-rounded education is the best way to prepare all students for any kind of work. Considering both perspectives, do you think schools should routinely adapt their curriculum to the changing job market? Why or why not?
content.post: Kelly: Andrew is right about the fast pace of today's job market shifts, but that’s just all the more reason for schools to be flexible. Not everyone plans further study after high school, and we need education systems that can quickly adapt and prepare students directly for the modern workforce. Otherwise, we risk being underprepared for future job demands.

writing.answer:
I agree with Kelly that schools should review their curriculum as the job market changes, but they should not replace foundational subjects every time a new trend appears. Reading, writing, mathematics, and scientific reasoning remain useful in almost any career. Still, students also need opportunities to learn skills that employers currently value, such as data literacy, teamwork, and the responsible use of artificial intelligence.

Andrew is right that schools cannot react as quickly as companies do. For that reason, a practical solution is to keep a stable academic core while updating electives and short project-based courses each year. Local employers and colleges could advise schools about emerging needs without controlling the entire curriculum.

This balanced approach would help students who enter the workforce immediately after high school, while also preparing those who continue their education. Routine review is valuable as long as schools distinguish lasting abilities from temporary hiring fashions.

speaking.answer: Oh, I love photography. I got my first camera two years ago as a birthday gift, and I've been taking pictures almost every weekend since then. Usually I walk around my city, uh, looking for interesting buildings, street scenes, or just good light in the evening. I especially love the golden hour, just before sunset, and I recently bought a small tripod for it. Sometimes I take friends along, and they pose for me. What I enjoy most is that it makes me notice details I'd normally miss, like the shadows on a wall or the expression on a stranger's face. I edit the best pictures on my laptop and share a few online. It's honestly a very relaxing way to spend time, and it gets me outside and moving, which is good because I sit at a desk most of the week.

speaking.answer: I think the most common ones are playing basketball or soccer, watching television series, and playing mobile games. Um, in many cities, people also love going to parks in the evening to dance, walk, or practice tai chi. Cooking and trying new restaurants are very popular too. I think these activities appeal to many people for a few reasons. Most of them are cheap, so almost everyone can afford them. They're also social, which fits well with how people value family and friends. And, you know, after long days of study or work, people want something simple and relaxing. speaking.answer: I'd say photography helps me in a few ways. First, it's the best way for me to relax. After a long week of classes, I grab my camera, walk around the city, and after an hour or so my mind feels clear. Um, it also gives me a sense of challenge, because I keep trying to get better shots in difficult light, and each small improvement makes me proud. Beyond that, I think it's made me more patient. I've learned to wait for the right moment, and that attitude helps with studying too. Honestly, I also notice the world around me a lot more. speaking.answer: I agree, to a large extent. Lives today are really busy, and work or school often takes over everything. I notice it myself, uh, during exam weeks I can't even pick up my camera for days. Plus, phones make it harder, because after a long day it's easier to just scroll through videos than to start a hobby that needs effort. Many of my friends who work full time say they're too tired in the evening to do anything but rest. That said, I think it's possible to find time if you really want to. content.stimulusText: Your professor is teaching a class on art history. Write a post responding to the professor's question. Express and support your opinion. Make a contribution to the discussion in your own words. An effective response will contain at least 100 words. Next week, we will discuss the influence of public art on community identity. Public art, such as murals and sculptures, can enrich a community's cultural landscape and contribute to a sense of shared identity. Do you think public art plays a significant role in shaping community identity? Why or why not?
content.post: Paul: While public art can enhance a community's aesthetic appeal, its role in shaping community identity may be limited. Other factors, such as social programs and community events, have a more substantial impact on fostering a shared identity.

writing.answer:
I believe public art does play a significant role in shaping community identity, even if it is not the only factor. Claire is right that murals, sculptures, and other shared artworks can reflect local history and values in a visible way. When people repeatedly see art that tells their community’s story, it can create pride and a stronger sense of belonging.

Paul is also correct that social programs and community events matter. Schools, festivals, and neighborhood services often shape daily relationships more directly than a single artwork. Still, public art can support those relationships by giving people a common landmark and a shared visual language.

For example, a mural about local workers or immigrant families can make residents feel recognized and can become a place where people gather for photos, tours, or community meetings. That combination of meaning and visibility is why I think public art is more than decoration. It may not replace social programs, but it can meaningfully strengthen community identity.
